data.title: Why Buffalo Potash's First Mine Could Be Just The Beginning
data.description:
Saskatchewan-based potash stock, Buffalo Potash (TSXV:BUFF), could be building something much bigger than its first mine suggests.

The company’s Disley project is being developed in stages, beginning with what the company calls its initial production module or IPM, which is designed to produce around 125,000 tonnes of potash annually.

However, that is just the beginning.

Two proposed follow-on facilities could eventually take the project's planned annual production capacity to 1.125 million tonnes, making the initial module a relatively small part of Buffalo's longer-term ambitions.

The big question is whether Buffalo can use this initial development to establish the foundations for a much larger potash business.

Buffalo Potash’s first steps

Buffalo Potash has decided that rather than jumping into developing a mine capable of full production, it would instead start small.

The initial production module is a smaller-scale mining facility designed to produce around 125,000 tonnes of soluble-grade potash annually. This means that rather than committing to the full Disley project, it is choosing to start with a facility capable of providing initial cash flow, with lower capital requirements as it establishes the foundation for future expansion.

This module will use Buffalo’s patented horizontal line drive technology.

In simple terms, this approach involves drilling three horizontal wells along an underground potash seam. This approach promises lower upfront capital requirements, lower operating costs, more selective extraction, and less infrastructure requirements.

Progress has moved beyond the planning stage. Buffalo Potash has received approval to construct and operate the initial production module in October 2026, subsequently commencing brine injection, the first test of whether Buffalo can make its method work, as well as beginning site development.

First production remains targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

For Buffalo, getting this first facility operational could be an important step towards demonstrating the technology and supporting the case for a much larger Disley development.

How two more mines could transform Buffalo’s Disley Project

Buffalo Potash's real growth opportunity lies not in its initial production module, but in what the company plans to come after.

It plans to build two additional facilities, Disley East and Disley West, each designed to produce around 500,000 tonnes of potash annually. If both proceed, this would add 1 million tonnes of annual capacity, taking the Disley Project’s planned total production from 125,000 to 1.125 million tonnes. This would be a welcome addition to a market which is considered by many countries to be a critical mineral.

There is also a difference in what the facilities would produce.

While the IPM is designed to produce soluble-grade potash, the two larger operations are intended to produce granular muriate of potash (MOP), a more widely used fertiliser product. This would give Buffalo a pathway into a much larger-scale production operation, with the potential to contribute to the growing opportunity for Canadian potash producers.

The results of the IPM will go a long way in determining how successful and viable Buffalo’s expansion could be.

At full capacity, the two proposed mines would produce eight times as much potash as the initial module, illustrating just how much larger Buffalo's ambitions could become.

More than just a first mine

Buffalo’s long-term ambitions are vast, but much of it relies on the success of its initial production module.

Given that the Disley Project is located in Saskatchewan, which is already a major global hub of potash production, its proximity to major mines and infrastructure is a positive. But until it starts showing that it can produce potash profitably, such ambitions will remain largely potential rather than reality.

But that potential is there, and interest is already building, with the company announcing that seven state-owned enterprises and major private companies have reached out to Buffalo Potash seeking new sources of Potash supply.

The most-followed narrative in the Simply Wall St community for Buffalo Potash highlights the company's opportunity to bring new Canadian potash supply to market using a potentially lower-cost mining method. It also points to the recent regulatory approval and proposed C$8.5 million royalty funding agreement with Altius Minerals as important steps towards getting the first module operational.

There is no question that Buffalo’s ambition is large and that the opportunity is there given the increasing importance placed on potash as a key ingredient of fertilizer. Investors will, however, be focused on execution.

data.title: We Like The Quality Of Uniao Pet Participacoes' (BVMF:AUAU3) Earnings
data.description:
Uniao Pet Participacoes S.A.'s (BVMF:AUAU3) recent earnings report didn't offer any surprises, with the shares unchanged over the last week. We did some analysis to find out why and believe that investors might be missing some encouraging factors contained in the earnings.

A Closer Look At Uniao Pet Participacoes' Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Uniao Pet Participacoes has an accrual ratio of -0.33 for the year to September 2026. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of R$799m, well over the R$220.2m it reported in profit. Uniao Pet Participacoes shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Uniao Pet Participacoes' Profit Performance

Happily for shareholders, Uniao Pet Participacoes produced plenty of free cash flow to back up its statutory profit numbers. Because of this, we think Uniao Pet Participacoes' underlying earnings potential is as good as, or possibly even better, than the statutory profit makes it seem! With the stock now carrying a much larger market value than five years ago, the key issue is how that payout profile stacks up against the price you would be paying today.

  • Over the past 5 years Iberdrola has returned 160.9% which puts a lot of weight on the idea that its dividends can support a meaningfully higher valuation than in the past.

The issue now is whether Iberdrola's current share price is properly reflected by the dividend stream implied by its intrinsic value under the Dividend Discount Model (DDM).

If you are weighing Iberdrola's dividend story against other income-focused opportunities, it can help to compare it with companies in our 239 dividend fortresses

Does Iberdrola Look Pricey on Dividends?

The Dividend Discount Model (DDM) values Iberdrola by projecting its future dividend stream and discounting that back to today. On this view, the key inputs are how fast the payout can grow and how much of earnings management is willing to share with investors. The model uses a dividend per share of €0.81, a return on equity of about 9.5% and a payout ratio near 20%, which together translate into a capped dividend growth rate of 3.06% a year.

That relatively modest growth cap matters because Iberdrola trades at €22.59, while the DDM projections put Iberdrola's estimated intrinsic value meaningfully below the current share price. A low payout today combined with expected growth above 7% in earnings implies more cash being retained inside the business, not necessarily flowing out as higher dividends. Because Iberdrola and peers are committing large amounts to US offshore wind projects, those capital needs help explain why a dividend-focused model could point below the market price. For income investors comparing the yield and growth profile with alternatives, the DDM gap is a reminder to stress test how much dividend expansion really feels plausible over time.
